title: Political Parties and Pressure Groups
summary: In a representative democracy the people elect representatives, usually nominated by political parties. Parties are essential: they let people take part in elections, educate them and offer policy choices. Countries without parties, such as Libya, Oman, Qatar and the UAE, are not democracies.

A political party is an organised body of people who share common principles and goals and seek political power through constitutional means to put their policies into practice. Gilchrist: 'an organised group of citizens who profess the same political views and who, acting as a political unit, try to control the government'. Characteristics: an organised group; common principles and goals; aims at political power through collective effort; uses peaceful, constitutional methods — elections; converts its programme into government policy when in power.

Parties nominate candidates and campaign in elections; place their programmes before voters through manifestos; the majority party forms the government and implements policies; parties in minority form the opposition and keep a check on the government; they educate people and shape public opinion; articulate people's demands and convey them to the government; and link the people with government institutions. Indian parties have made representative government possible since independence.

The Indian National Congress (1885) began as an umbrella organisation; the Muslim League, Communist Party and Hindu Mahasabha also arose before independence. After 1947 the Congress dominated till 1967 (1952, 1957, 1962, 1967) — the 'one-party dominant system'. From 1967 the system changed; after 1977 the Janata Party government briefly suggested a two-party system. Since 1989 India has had coalition governments at the Centre; since 1999 two broad alliances — the BJP-led NDA and the Congress-led UPA. India now has a multi-party system.

Features today: many parties compete; a bi-nodal pattern around the Congress and BJP; regional parties play a vital role in forming Central governments and win favours for their States; elections are fought between coalitions; there are no permanent rulers or opposition; ideology has taken a back seat to a Common Minimum Programme and pragmatism; parties use emotive slogans ('Garibi Hatao', 'India Shining', 'Aam Aadmi') and chase short-term gains.

The Election Commission classifies parties as National, State and Registered (unrecognised), and allots election symbols to parties and candidates. A national party must be recognised in four or more States, or win a set share of Lok Sabha seats/votes (the textbook gives: at least 4% of Lok Sabha seats or 3.33% of assembly seats, and 6% of valid votes). In 2009 there were 7 national parties (Congress, BJP, CPI, CPI(M), BSP, NCP, RJD — the list changes; today, for example, the Aam Aadmi Party is national and the RJD is not), 34 State parties and 322 registered parties.

Policies: Congress (1885) — democracy, secularism, socialism; centrist; supports liberalisation (LPG) with welfare of weaker sections. BJP (1980, successor of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh) — nationalism and national integration, democracy, positive secularism, Gandhian socialism, value-based politics. Communist parties — CPI (1925) and CPI(M) (1964), based on Marxism-Leninism; for workers and peasants, socialism, land reforms; against capitalism and globalisation; ruled West Bengal, Kerala and Tripura. BSP (1984, Kanshi Ram; led by Mayawati) — for Dalits and the deprived, inspired by Phule, Periyar and Ambedkar; 'Sarvajan Hitay, Sarvajan Sukhay'. NCP (1999, Sharad Pawar, P.A. Sangma, Tariq Anwar; base in Maharashtra). RJD (1997, Lalu Prasad Yadav; Bihar) — social justice for backward castes and minorities.

Regional parties arose to fulfil regional aspirations: Trinamool Congress (West Bengal), Asom Gana Parishad (Assam), AIADMK and DMK (Tamil Nadu), National Conference (J&K), Samajwadi Party (UP), Shiromani Akali Dal (Punjab), Shiv Sena (Maharashtra), Telugu Desam (Andhra Pradesh). They have federalised the party system and strengthened cooperative federalism.

Interest groups are organised groups seeking to promote specific interests of their members; when they put pressure on the government to get their demands met, they become pressure groups. So all pressure groups are interest groups, but not all interest groups are pressure groups. Interest groups are formally organised, interest-oriented, softer and may or may not influence policy; pressure groups are strictly structured, pressure-focused, harsher and must influence policy.

Pressure groups differ from parties: they are not primarily political (e.g. the RSS is a cultural organisation), do not seek power directly, do not contest elections, need not have an ideology, and have specific interests, whereas parties seek power, contest elections, have ideologies and national programmes. Some are linked to parties (NSUI–Congress, ABVP–BJP; trade unions). Methods: appeals, petitions, demonstrations, picketing, lobbying, processions, media campaigns, satyagraha, strikes and boycotts. Examples in India: religious and caste groups, FICCI, AITUC, Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh, Kisan Sabha, government employees' unions, All Assam Students' Union.

CSOs are bodies formed by citizens on issues of common concern — environment, price rise, corruption, gender, child labour — and are a new form of mass pressure. Examples: Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (Aruna Roy; led the movement for the Right to Information law), SEWA (Ela Bhatt; rights of women workers), Narmada Bachao Andolan (Medha Patkar), India Against Corruption (Anna Hazare), PUCL, NAPM, NAWO and the Meira Paibis of Manipur (supporting Irom Sharmila's long fast against AFSPA). They channel grievances, point out unfulfilled promises and train good, vigilant citizens.

vsa: Why does a political party aim to achieve power? Explain.

(1) A political party is generally described as an organized body of people who share common principles and cherish certain common goals regarding the political system. Every political party pronounces its policies and programmes as commitment to the electorate. (2) The political parties seek power to form the government.

or: Why is the Indian party system called a multi-party system? Explain.

(1) Many national, State and registered parties compete for power; no single party usually wins a majority, so national parties depend on regional parties and form coalition governments (NDA, UPA). (2) We can, therefore, say that democracy in India has been strengthened by a competitive and multi-party system. In general, the party system in India has not been a fixed one like a single party system or a dominant one-party system or a two-party system or a multiparty system.

Explain two characteristics of a political party.

(1) the organized group of people believe in common principles and common goals; (2) A political party operates and seeks political power through constitutional means to translate its policies into practice. it employs constitutional and peaceful methods in seeking control over the government through elections; and
Mention the conditions required to be recognised as a national political party.

(1) Political parties in India are classified by the Election Commission for the allocation of symbols. In general, these groups try to press upon the government for formulation of policies or enactment of laws according to their interests. Some characteristics of interest groups, pressure groups and political parties are given below in a jumbled form. (2) It should be a recognized political party in four or more states. (3) It should have won at least 4 per cent of the seats in the last Lok Sabha elections or 3.33 per cent of the seats in the assembly elections from the state. All the candidates put by the party should have polled at least 6 per cent of the total valid votes in the elections.
How do political parties help in running democratic processes?

(1) Political parties actually help the institutions and processes of a government democratic. They enable people to participate in elections and other processes of governance, educate them and facilitate them to make policy choices. (2) They place objectives and programmes before the voters through their manifestos; those securing the majority in elections form the government and enact and implement the policies; they educate people and help in formulating and shaping public opinion.
Why are Civil Society Organisations considered a new form of mass pressure tactics? Two points.

(1) Civil Society Organizations are formed by such vigilant citizens. These organizations are run by ordinary persons who feel strongly committed to certain issues. (2) Such organizations put pressure on the government for changing policies on many important issues such as corruption, human rights, livelihood of different people, environmental protection, women empowerment, educational and health issues. They point out when the government is not fulfilling its promises to the nation.
sa: Explain any three challenges faced by political parties in India.

(1) Lack of internal democracy and dynastic succession — power stays with a few leaders and families. (2) Growing role of money and muscle power and criminalisation of politics. (3) Coalition compulsions and frequent switching of alliances make parties focus on short-term gains and emotive issues rather than ideology and lasting policies.
Explain, with examples, the role of pressure groups.

(1) they educate people and help in formulating and shaping public opinion; For example, the trade unions help their respective political parties by providing them workers during elections. They help promote, discuss, debate and mobilize public opinion on major public issues. (2) They press the government through petitions, lobbying, demonstrations, satyagraha and strikes — e.g. FICCI on industrial policy, Kisan Sabhas on farm prices. (3) These groups try to bring changes in public policy. For instance, the Self-Employed Women’s Association (SEWA) has influenced the government to improve its policies on the rights of women workers. Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan led the people’s movement which got the government to bring about the law on ‘Right to Information’.
Differentiate between national and regional political parties with examples.

(1) A national party should be a recognized political party in four or more states. National Parties- 7 (Congress, BJP, CPM, CPI, BSP, Nationalist Congress Party and Rashtriya Janata Dal). (2) Regional political parties have emerged to fulfill regional aspirations. The regional political parties include, among others, the Akali Dal (Punjab), the DMK and the AIADMK (Tamil Nadu), the Telugu Desam (Andhra Pradesh), the National Conference (Jammu and Kashmir), the Shiv Sena (Maharashtra), the Trinamool Congress (West Bengal). (3) National parties take up national and international issues, while regional parties focus on their State's interests and often support coalitions at the Centre.
How are pressure groups different from political parties? Explain.

(1) Pressure groups are not primarily political in nature. The political parties seek power to form the government. (2) Pressure groups do not necessarily have political ideologies. Political parties nominate candidates, contest elections, and participate in elections campaigns. (3) Pressure groups have specific, limited interests and may have no ideology; parties have ideologies and broad national programmes.
Differentiate between pressure groups and interest groups.

(1) These are called pressure groups or interest groups. An interest group that exerts pressure on the government to achieve its goals is called a pressure group. A pressure group is an interest group which exerts pressure on the government or the decision-makers for the fulfillment of the interests of its members. (2) Pressure groups do not necessarily have political ideologies. (3) Interest groups are softer and more protective; pressure groups are strictly structured, harsher and both protective and promotive. All pressure groups are interest groups, but not all interest groups are pressure groups.
Explain the importance of regional political parties in India.

(1) Regional political parties have emerged to fulfill regional aspirations. (2) The regional political parties have come to play a vital role in the formation of governments at the Centre. (3) It is because of the regional political parties that our party-system has been federalized. The evolving nature of our party system has strengthened the cooperative trends of our federal system.
la: Explain any six functions of political parties in India.

(1) Political parties nominate candidates, contest elections, and participate in elections campaigns. (2) they campaign to obtain support for their candidates in the elections; It remained a dominant political party up to 1967, as it continued to win elections held in 1952, 1957, 1962 and 1967 at the Centre as well as in almost all the States. (3) they place objectives and programmes before the voters through their manifestos; those securing the majority in elections form the government and enact and implement the policies; (4) Indian party system witnesses a coalition system of government from 1989 onwards. May or may not influence the policies of the government People’s participation in the election is what makes our democracy a representative and participatory democracy. Public opinion is not the unanimous opinion of the people, nor it is the opinion of the majority. (5) Those not in power form opposition and keep a constant check on the government; they form opposition when they are in minority in the legislature and constantly put pressure on the government for proper governance; (6) they educate people and help in formulating and shaping public opinion; they articulate peoples’ demands and convey them to the government; and

or: What are Civil Society Organisations? Write the names of any four contemporary Civil Society Organisations in India.

(1) CSOs are associations, groups and voluntary agencies formed by citizens to pursue issues of common concern — environment, corruption, price rise, gender justice, child labour — acting as an interface between the State and the individual and pressing the government to change policies. (2) Some important leaders of Civil Society Organizations in recent times include Aruna Roy (Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan), Ela Bhatt (Self-employed Women’s Association), Medha Patkar (Narmada Bachao Andolan) and Anna Hazare (India Against Corruption).

la: Suggest any six effective measures to reform political parties.

(1) Ensure internal democracy — regular organisational elections within parties. (2) Make party finances transparent and audit them; limit election expenses. (3) Keep candidates with criminal records out of elections. (4) Enforce the anti-defection law to stop party-switching for gain. (5) Give fair representation to women and weaker sections in tickets and posts. (6) Encourage parties to campaign on policies and programmes rather than caste, religion and emotive slogans, and let citizens and the media keep a check.
